# The application layer {#sec-07-application}

Chapter 6 mapped the five layers; from now on we descend through them,
one per chapter, and we begin at the top — where your programs actually
talk to each other. Everything below the application layer exists to
carry these conversations. The plan mirrors a real page load: First how
communicating programs are arranged at all, then how a name becomes an
address (DNS), then the conversation itself (HTTP), and finally the two
other classics — e-mail and file transfer — with the security lesson that
all of them teach: Encrypt by default.

## Application architectures {#sec-07-architectures}

The application layer is where *your* software lives — browsers, mail
clients, games, apps. Each application defines a protocol
(@def-protocol): An agreed conversation between its parts. It does not
move bytes itself; it hands them to the transport layer below. The
examples of this chapter — HTTP, DNS, SMTP, FTP — are each a different
conversation for a different job, but almost all of them follow one of
two shapes.

::: {#def-clientserver}
## Client/server and peer-to-peer
In a **client/server** architecture, one side — the client — takes the
initiative and requests a service; the other — the server — is always on,
has a fixed address, and delivers it. In a **peer-to-peer** (P2P)
architecture, every machine is both client and server at once.
:::

Most of the web is client/server: Your browser is a client; the website
runs on servers. P2P has real advantages — no always-on central servers
needed, and it *self-scales*, since more users bring more capacity — and
real drawbacks: Security and reliability are hard in distributed systems,
peers come and go unpredictably, and the model's history is entangled
with unmanaged file sharing. Classic P2P: File-sharing networks, and
parts of blockchains today. Many real systems mix the two shapes into
*hybrids*: Skype, Teams and their kin use a central server to solve the
hard "where are you?" problem — looking up the other party's address —
and then run the actual call peer-to-peer, directly between the two
machines, saving the server's bandwidth.

One more idea prepares next week. Different applications make very
different demands on the network below: Audio and video tolerate data
loss (a glitch is fine) but demand timing; file transfer and banking
tolerate delay but allow no loss at all; streaming needs a minimum
bandwidth where e-mail works at any speed. These needs shape which
transport protocol an application chooses in Chapter 8 — reliable TCP, or
fast-and-lean UDP.

## DNS: Names to addresses {#sec-07-dns}

Before any program connects, a name must become an address: You type
`www.kristiania.no`; the network needs an IP address. People remember
names; machines route by numbers.

::: {#def-dns}
## DNS
The **Domain Name System** translates domain names into IP addresses —
the internet's phone book, and the first step of almost every connection.
It is deliberately *distributed*: No single server holds every name; the
data is spread worldwide across a hierarchy, so there is no single point
of failure and no machine drowning in the world's lookups.
:::

The hierarchy is a tree. At the top, the *root* (thirteen root server
identities worldwide) points to the *top-level domain* (TLD) servers —
`.com`, `.no`, `.org` — which point in turn to each organisation's own
*authoritative* server.

::: {#exm-dnsresolve}
## Resolving a name, step by step
Your machine does not walk the tree itself; it asks its *local resolver*,
which does. (1) Your PC asks the resolver for `www.kristiania.no`.
(2) The resolver asks the root — answer: "ask `.no`"; asks the `.no` TLD
server — "ask Kristiania's server"; asks Kristiania's authoritative
server — which returns the IP. (3) The resolver hands the address back,
and your browser can connect. Doing this walk for every single lookup
would be slow, so answers are remembered: Resolvers *cache* what they
have looked up, and every record carries a TTL (time-to-live) saying how
long it may be cached. That is why a changed DNS record takes a while to
"spread": Old answers live on in caches until their TTL runs out.
:::

![Resolving `www.kristiania.no`: Your PC asks the local resolver (1); the resolver walks root, TLD and authoritative server (2–4) and returns — and caches — the answer (5).](figures/fig-dnswalk.svg){#fig-dnswalk}

What exactly is stored? DNS is a distributed database of small typed
*resource records*, each with four fields — name, value, type, TTL. The
types to know: `A` maps a name to an IPv4 address; `AAAA` to an IPv6
address; `CNAME` declares an alias for another name; `MX` names the mail
server for a domain; `NS` names the authoritative name server. So DNS
does more than addresses — an `MX` record is how e-mail finds the right
server, as @sec-07-email uses. And all of it is queryable by hand, which
is the best way to make the theory concrete: `nslookup www.kristiania.no`
for the address behind a name; `dig kristiania.no MX` for a domain's mail
servers; and `dig +trace` to watch the resolver's walk — root, TLD,
authoritative — appear answer by answer.

::: {.callout-note title="Excursus — Recursive, iterative, and the domain that runs backwards"}
Two details from the standard reference sharpen the resolution story.
First, the two roles in @exm-dnsresolve have proper names: Your PC sends
a *recursive* query — "get me the final answer, do the work yourself" —
and the resolver, in turn, asks the root, TLD and authoritative servers
*iterative* queries, each answered only with a referral to the next
server. A flag bit in every DNS message (*recursion desired*) requests
the first behaviour, and the busy root and TLD servers simply refuse it —
they refer, and never chase answers for anyone. Second, DNS can also run
backwards: To turn an IP address into a name, a special domain
`in-addr.arpa` holds the address bytes *in reverse order* — the name
behind `158.36.10.4` is looked up as `4.10.36.158.in-addr.arpa` — so that
the address's network part, like any domain, sits at the right-hand,
delegatable end. This *reverse DNS* is what `traceroute` uses to print
router names instead of bare addresses.

*(Dostálek & Kabelová, 2006, ch. 11)*
:::

## The web and HTTP {#sec-07-http}

With the address in hand, the browser can finally talk to the server. The
browser is the client half of a web application: It understands HTML
(structure), CSS (style) and JavaScript (behaviour), and one "page"
usually means *many* requests — text, images, scripts, fonts. Open the
developer tools (Ctrl-Shift-I in Chrome), reload any page, and watch the
requests fly; each one is a single HTTP exchange.

::: {#def-http}
## HTTP
The Hypertext Transfer Protocol is a client/server conversation over TCP:
The browser opens a TCP connection (a *socket*) to the server's port — 80
for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS — sends a *request*, and reads the *response*.
Both are plain text: A first line, some headers, then a body.
:::

::: {#exm-httpexchange}
## One exchange, for real
The request:

```default
GET /index.html HTTP/1.1
Host: www.kristiania.no
User-Agent: Firefox
Accept: text/html
```

The response:

```default
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 1024

<html>...</html>
```

Method and path drive the request; the status line opens the response;
headers describe each side's payload. Nothing here is binary mystery — it
is text you could type.
:::

The path and host in that request came from a URL, which packs several
pieces into one string. In
`https://www.example.org:443/a/b/c.txt?t=win&s=chess#p5`: The *scheme*
(`https`) names the protocol; the *authority* (`www.example.org`) is the
host, resolved by DNS; the *port* (`:443`) is often implied by the
scheme; then the *path* to the resource, the *query* parameters after the
`?`, and the *fragment* after the `#` — a spot within the page.

::: {.callout-tip title="Worked exercise 7.1 — Take a URL apart"}
Decompose the URL

```default
https://api.example.com/v2/users?id=7&lang=no#profile
```

into its components — and say which component DNS resolves, and which
component the request line of @exm-httpexchange carries.

**Solution.** Scheme `https` (so port 443 implied); host
`api.example.com`; path `/v2/users`; query `id=7&lang=no`; fragment
`profile`. DNS resolves the *host*; the request line carries the *path*
(plus query) —

```default
GET /v2/users?id=7&lang=no HTTP/1.1
```

— while the host travels in the `Host:` header.
:::

The first word of the request is the *method*, the verb saying what you
want done with the resource: `GET` fetches, `POST` sends data to the
server, `HEAD` asks only for the headers, `PUT` uploads to the given URL,
`DELETE` removes it — with `GET` and `POST` covering almost all everyday
browsing. The response's first line carries a three-digit *status code*
whose first digit gives the category: 1xx informational; 2xx success (200
OK); 3xx redirection (301 Moved); 4xx client error — including the famous
404 Not Found, which simply means the client asked for something the
server does not have; 5xx server error (500 Internal Error).

One design decision of HTTP has consequences you meet daily: HTTP itself
is *stateless* — by default, each request is independent and the server
forgets you afterwards. So how do logins and shopping carts survive
between requests? Through *cookies*: The server sends a `Set-Cookie`
header; the browser stores the value and returns it in a `Cookie` header
on later requests, letting the site recognise you. Cookies can be
persistent (stored until an expiry date) or last only for the current
session.

Everything so far crosses the wire as readable text — and Chapter 6's
Wireshark showed what that means on a shared network: Anyone on the path
could read it. **HTTPS** closes the hole: It is *ordinary HTTP carried
over a TLS-encrypted transport connection*, protecting the content and
confirming you are talking to the real server — default port 443, the
padlock in the address bar, and the web's default today. Finally, HTTP
itself has evolved, each version removing a bottleneck of the one before:
HTTP/0.9 (1991) knew only one-line `GET`; HTTP/1.0 (1996) added headers,
status codes, `POST` and `HEAD`; HTTP/1.1 (1997) added persistent
connections that reuse the TCP link; HTTP/2 (2015) multiplexes many
requests on one connection; HTTP/3 (2022) runs over QUIC, on UDP, for
faster setup. The trend in one line: Fewer round-trips, more parallelism
— the same conversation, delivered quicker.

## E-mail {#sec-07-email}

E-mail is older than the web and still everywhere, and it separates
cleanly into three parts: A *user agent* to read and write mail (Outlook,
Apple Mail, …), a *mail server* that holds your inbox and a queue of
outgoing mail, and the protocols that move messages between them. The
division of labour is the thing to learn: **SMTP** carries mail *towards*
the recipient — user agent to server, and server to server — while
**IMAP** or **POP3** fetch it back from the server to your devices.

SMTP, the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, uses TCP (default ports 587 for
submission by clients and 25 between servers) and runs a short scripted
conversation — `HELO`, `MAIL FROM:`, `RCPT TO:`, `DATA` — after which the
message body follows, ending with a single "`.`" on a line of its own.
The word that captures SMTP's character: It *pushes* — the sender drives
the data towards the recipient's server. Collection is the second
protocol's job, and the two options split by lifestyle: POP3 is simple —
authorise, download to the client, often removing mail from the server
afterwards — and fits a single machine; IMAP keeps mail *on* the server,
organised in folders, so the same mailbox stays in sync across devices —
the natural fit for today's phone-plus-laptop world.

![The division of labour in e-mail: SMTP pushes the message towards the recipient's server, hop by hop; IMAP or POP3 pull it from there to the recipient's devices.](figures/fig-mailflow.svg){#fig-mailflow}

Set SMTP beside HTTP and the contrast teaches both: SMTP pushes data to
the receiver, HTTP *pulls* it on request; SMTP holds one persistent
connection and packs many objects into one message, classic HTTP opened a
connection per request and carried one resource each; SMTP's message
format is 7-bit ASCII — binary attachments travel base64-encoded via MIME
— while HTTP bodies carry any bytes. Same layer, same TCP underneath, but
each shaped by what it was designed to do.

## File transfer, and the security lesson {#sec-07-ftp}

The last classic job is moving whole files, and its traditional protocol
has an unusual shape worth knowing.

::: {#def-ftp}
## FTP
The File Transfer Protocol separates commands from data: A **control
connection** on TCP port 21 carries the commands, while a *separate data
connection* carries the files themselves. FTP is *stateful*: The server
remembers the session — your login, your current folder — between
commands.
:::

The command set over the control channel is small: `user` and `pass` to
log in, `dir`/`ls` to list files, `get` to download, `put` to upload. A
graphical client like FileZilla wraps these in drag-and-drop — but the
same commands run underneath, and in the Practice you will speak them
yourself against a real FTP server and watch the two connections appear.

Now the lesson the whole chapter has been building towards. Plain FTP
sends everything — *including your password* — in the clear; plain HTTP
sends your pages likewise. Their secure successors differ in mechanism
but agree in spirit: **SFTP** is a different protocol (not "FTP with an
S") that runs file transfer over *SSH*, encrypted end to end; **HTTPS**
is HTTP over *TLS*, as above. The general rule deserves italics: *Any
plaintext protocol can be read by someone on the path; modern practice is
to encrypt by default.* When Wireshark shows you a plaintext FTP login in
the lab, the rule will stop being abstract.

**Before Lecture 8 (The transport layer).** Read the Module 8 chapter in
the textbook (`Readings.xlsx` for the pages). Try this: In your browser's
developer tools, open the Network tab and reload a page — count the
requests behind one "page". And think about the question that opens next
week: HTTP needs every byte to arrive in order; a video call does not.
Should they really use the same delivery service underneath?

## Summary {#sec-07-summary}

Applications are arranged client/server or peer-to-peer
(@def-clientserver), with hybrids using a server to find each other and
direct connections for the heavy data. Before anything connects, DNS
(@def-dns) turns names into addresses through a distributed hierarchy —
root, TLD, authoritative — softened by caching and TTLs, and carrying
typed records (`A`, `AAAA`, `CNAME`, `MX`, `NS`) that do more than
addressing. HTTP (@def-http, @exm-httpexchange) fetches the web in
plain-text request/response pairs — methods, status codes, URLs — with
cookies supplying the state that the protocol itself deliberately lacks,
and versions 1.1, 2 and 3 trimming round-trips. E-mail splits into user
agent, server and two protocol roles: SMTP pushes mail towards the
recipient, POP3 or IMAP pulls it back. FTP (@def-ftp) moves files over
separate control and data connections — and, like plain HTTP, in the
clear, which is why SFTP (over SSH) and HTTPS (over TLS) exist and why
the chapter's closing rule is *encrypt by default*. Next week we drop one
layer: How all these conversations are actually delivered.

## Self-check {#sec-07-self-check .unnumbered}

::: {#exr-07-hybrid}
## Hybrid architectures
Skype-like systems are called hybrid architectures. What exactly does the
central server do, what runs peer-to-peer, and why is that split
efficient?
:::

::: {#exr-07-resolve}
## Resolving a name
Walk through the resolution of a name your resolver has never seen: Which
three servers answer, in which order, and what does each answer say? Then
explain why the second lookup of the same name is faster.
:::

::: {#exr-07-url}
## URL components
Decompose `https://shop.example.no:443/varer/sko.html?size=42#top` into
its six URL components.
:::

::: {#exr-07-status}
## Status codes and statelessness
Your browser shows a 404 on one page and a 500 on another. Whose fault is
each, by category — and what does statelessness mean for the request you
send right after?
:::

::: {#exr-07-mail}
## The mail protocols
In one sentence each: What does SMTP do, what do POP3/IMAP do, and which
of the two collection protocols suits someone reading mail on a phone and
a laptop?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Sketch answers
(1) The server only answers "where is the other party?" — the lookup; the
call's audio and video then flow directly between the peers, so the heavy
bandwidth never touches the server. (2) Root ("ask the TLD"), then the
TLD server ("ask the organisation's authoritative server"), then the
authoritative server (the IP itself); the resolver caches the answer, so
the second lookup is served locally until the record's TTL expires.
(3) Scheme `https`; host `shop.example.no`; port `443`; path
`/varer/sko.html`; query `size=42`; fragment `top`. (4) 404 is a 4xx —
client error: The thing asked for does not exist there; 500 is a 5xx —
server error: The server failed while handling a valid request.
Statelessness means the next request is independent — the server has
forgotten the exchange, unless a cookie carries the state back. (5) SMTP
pushes mail towards the recipient's server; POP3/IMAP fetch it from that
server to your devices; IMAP — it keeps the mailbox on the server and in
sync across devices.
:::

::: {.bridge}
Applications now talk: Names resolve, pages load, mail moves — but every
protocol of this chapter quietly assumed that its bytes would arrive, and
arrive in order. Chapter 8 examines the layer that makes that promise —
or deliberately declines to: Transport, with ports to find the right
process and the TCP-versus-UDP choice that this chapter's applications
demanded.
:::
